notes.meaning: Immediately after His baptism, the Holy Spirit leads Jesus into the barren desert to face testing from the devil. God arranged this spiritual battle to test and prove the Messiah's character and faithful obedience. Unlike Adam in the garden and Israel in the desert, Jesus remained completely loyal to God under trial.

Jesus went without any food for forty days and forty nights, matching the long fasts of Moses and Elijah in the Old Testament. During these weeks of intense communion with God, His physical needs were supernaturally sustained. When the fast finally ended, He felt deep and severe human hunger.

differ.view: Christians should not view Christ's miraculous fast as a required pattern of self-denial for believers to copy on their own initiative.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The forty days of Lent are kept as a churchwide season of fasting and spiritual preparation modeled on Jesus' forty days in the wilderness.

notes.meaning: Satan comes to Jesus at His weakest physical moment, challenging Him to turn desert stones into loaves of bread if He really is God's Son. The devil wanted Jesus to doubt His Father's loving care and take matters into His own hands. He urged Him to misuse His divine power for personal relief instead of waiting on God.

Jesus answers by quoting Deuteronomy, declaring that human life depends on far more than ordinary bread. Real life comes from trusting every word and promise that God speaks. Instead of doing a self-serving miracle, Jesus chose complete obedience and trust in His Father's provision.

The devil then takes Jesus into Jerusalem, known as the holy city because God's presence and worship were centered there. He places Jesus on the pinnacle, a very high roof or battlement of the temple overlooking a steep valley. From this dizzying height, Satan prepares to tempt Jesus a second time.

Satan dares Jesus to leap into the air, quoting Psalm 91 to argue that God will command angels to protect Him from hitting the ground. The devil twisted God's promise of safety into an excuse for reckless pride and public showmanship. He tried to trick Jesus into staging a dramatic spectacle to force God to rescue Him.

Jesus counters the devil's quote with another command from Deuteronomy: never put the Lord your God to the test. God promises to protect His children in life's duties, but not when they intentionally walk into danger just to see what He will do. True trust never demands miracles or tests God's faithfulness through foolish stunts.

Next, the devil brings Jesus up to a very high mountain to display all the kingdoms of the earth and their splendor. In this sweeping vision, Satan showed all the wealth, power, and glory that human rulers seek after. He presented earthly greatness as something within Jesus' easy reach.

Satan offers to hand over all these kingdoms if Jesus will only kneel down and give him worship. This was a tempting shortcut around the pain and suffering of the cross. The devil brazenly asked the true King of heaven to give homage to an evil creature.

Jesus directly orders the tempter away, calling him Satan for the first time with divine authority. He quotes the law of Moses, stating that worship and wholehearted service belong exclusively to God. By standing firm on Scripture, Jesus refused worldly dominion at the cost of disloyalty to His Father.

Having exhausted his schemes, the devil leaves Jesus alone for a time. Heavenly angels then arrive to serve Christ, providing the comfort, care, and food He had refused to grab for Himself. Jesus' lonely victory proved He was the sinless and obedient Son of God.

Jesus learns that John the Baptist has been arrested and thrown into prison by King Herod Antipas. Rather than staying in Judea, Jesus travels north into the region of Galilee. He moved not out of cowardice, but because God's timetable called for the start of His own widespread Galilean ministry.

Leaving His childhood hometown of Nazareth, Jesus relocates His home to Capernaum, a thriving fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee. This town lay in the ancient tribal lands of Zebulun and Naphtali. Capernaum provided a busy crossroads where His message could reach many local Jews and visiting Gentiles.

Matthew points out that Jesus' move to Capernaum was not a random choice or mere accident. It directly fulfilled an ancient prophecy written hundreds of years earlier through the prophet Isaiah. God was guiding every detail of the Messiah's location according to His promised plan.

Isaiah's prophecy singled out the northern border lands of Zebulun and Naphtali along the sea road and the Jordan River. This region was known as Galilee of the Gentiles because many foreign nations lived there alongside Jews. Though often looked down upon by people in Jerusalem, this territory was chosen to receive the Messiah.

The people living in this northern country were trapped in deep spiritual blindness and the dark shadow of death. When Jesus arrived with His teaching and power, a radiant light of hope and rescue burst into their gloom. His presence brought spiritual life where there had only been ignorance and sin.

Jesus begins His public preaching with an urgent summons: people must repent, because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. To repent means to change one's mind, turn away from sin, and turn toward God. Jesus announced that God's long-awaited royal rule was breaking into human history through His own arrival.

While walking along the shoreline of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees two brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew. They were busy throwing circular fishing nets into the water, working at their trade. Jesus chose ordinary, hardworking laborers rather than famous scholars or wealthy leaders to be His closest followers.

Jesus calls out to them to follow Him, promising to transform them into fishers of men. To follow a master meant sharing His life, learning His teaching, and adopting His ways. Instead of gathering fish from the lake, they would now be trained to bring lost people into God's saving kingdom.

Peter and Andrew do not delay or hesitate, but leave their fishing nets behind at once to go with Jesus. Their instant action showed genuine faith in His authority and a willingness to surrender their livelihood for His mission. When Christ calls, He looks for prompt and wholehearted obedience.

Going a little further down the beach, Jesus notices two other brothers, James and John. They were sitting inside a fishing boat with their father Zebedee, actively mending and preparing their nets for use. Jesus issues the same life-changing call to them.

James and John immediately leave the family fishing boat, the workers, and their father to follow Jesus. Their swift decision showed that loyalty to Christ takes priority even over family businesses and home ties. They gladly sacrificed their security to give their lives to God's work.

Jesus travels throughout the whole province of Galilee, focusing on three great works: teaching, preaching, and healing. Synagogues were local Jewish meeting houses used for prayer, community gatherings, and studying the Scriptures. Jesus proclaimed the good news of God's coming kingdom and cured every sickness to prove His divine mercy and power.

Reports about Jesus' amazing words and deeds quickly spread far beyond Galilee into the wider territory of Syria. Crowds brought Him everyone who was suffering, including people with severe pain, evil spirits, seizures, and paralysis. Jesus healed them all, demonstrating that no human illness or spiritual bondage is beyond His power.

Huge crowds of people began following Jesus wherever He went. They arrived from Galilee, Jerusalem, Judea, regions across the Jordan River, and the Decapolis, a federation of ten largely Greek cities. People from every background, both Jews and Gentiles, gathered in excitement to witness His teaching and compassion.
